title: Signatures & const drill
intro: Rapid-fire: for each card, decide whether it **compiles** together with the section's *Given* code. Keys: **C** = compiles, **E** = error, **Enter** = next. After answering you can see what the real compiler says. Every answer here is checked by the compiler in `verify-content`, so none of them is a guess.

sections.title: Reading `const` with pointers
sections.rule: Read the declaration **right to left**, starting at the name. A `const` **left of `*`** protects the **pointee**: you can't modify it *through this pointer*. A `const` **right of `*`** protects the **pointer itself**: it can't be re-aimed. References only have the first kind.

cards.explanation: `p` is a *pointer to const int*: you can't modify the pointee **through `p`**. (`x` itself isn't const: `x = 5;` would be fine.)
The `const` is left of `*`, so it protects the int, not the pointer. Re-aiming `p` is allowed.
Read right to left: `p` is a **const pointer** to int. The pointer is fixed, but the int it points to can be modified.
`p` is a const pointer: once aimed, it can't be re-aimed.
`int const*` is exactly `const int*`. Only the position of `const` **relative to `*`** matters.
A const object must be initialised. A const pointer has to be aimed when it's created.
A *pointer to const* is not itself const, so it can be left uninitialised (but don't dereference it before aiming it).
Const on both sides: neither the pointee nor the pointer can change.

cards.code:
const int* const p = &cx;
int v = *p;
cards.explanation: Reading is always allowed. `const` only forbids writing.
`&cx` has type `const int*`. Storing it in an `int*` would let you modify a const, i.e. **remove** const. Never implicit.
The types match: a read-only view of a read-only int.

cards.code:
int* p = &x;
const int* q = p;
cards.explanation: **Adding** const is always allowed: `q` is a read-only view of `x`.

cards.code:
const int* q = &x;
int* p = q;
cards.explanation: Removing const is never implicit. `x` isn't const, but the compiler only knows `q`'s type: `const int*`.

cards.code:
int* const p = &x;
int* q = p;
cards.explanation: This copies the **value** of the pointer (an address) into a new pointer. The `const` was about `p` itself, not about the int, so nothing is lost.
`p` is a read-only *view*. It doesn't freeze `x`, which can still change by other paths. "Pointer to const" means "I won't modify it through here", not "this data is constant".
Same rule for references: a non-const `int&` to a `const int` would allow modifying it.
`r` is a read-only alias of `x`, so you can't assign through it.
A plain reference is just another name for `x`: this sets `x` to 4.

sections.title: Passing arguments: which calls compile?
sections.rule: **You can add `const`, never remove it.** A temporary (`42`, `x + 1`, `make()`) binds to a by-value parameter, a `const T&` or a `T&&`, but **never** to a plain `T&`. It also has no address to take with `&`.

cards.explanation: By value: the function gets its own copy. It accepts anything convertible to `int`.
A copy of a const is a fresh, modifiable `int`, so passing by value never conflicts with `const`.
Temporaries can be copied too.
`r` becomes another name for `x`. The function can modify the caller's variable.
`byRef` could modify `r`, i.e. `cx`. Binding `int&` to a `const int` would **remove const**.
A non-const reference can't bind to a temporary (an rvalue). Modifying "the 42" would be meaningless.
`x + 1` is a temporary value, not a variable. Same reason as `byRef(42)`.
A function returning `int` by value yields a temporary, which can't bind to `int&`.
Adding const is fine: the function just promises not to modify `x`.
A const alias of a const object.
Special rule: a **`const&` can bind to a temporary**, which lives until the end of the call. That's why `const T&` is the default for read-only parameters: it accepts *everything*, with no copy.
Same rule: `const int&` accepts temporaries.
`&x` has type `int*`, which matches exactly.
`byPtr` wants an **address**, and `x` is an `int`. Write `byPtr(&x)`. Unlike references, pointers make the `&` visible at the call site.
`&cx` is a `const int*`. Passing it as `int*` would remove const.
A `const int*` parameter accepts the address of a const.
`int*` → `const int*` adds const, which is always allowed.
A temporary has no address: `&` needs an lvalue.
A pointer parameter can receive "no object". That is **the** reason to choose `T*` over `T&`.
There is no null reference: a reference always names an existing object.
`*p` is an lvalue naming `x`, so it binds to `int&` (and `byRef` can modify `x`).
Seen through `q`, `*q` has type `const int`. Binding it to `int&` would remove const.
A reference is just another name for `x`, so `&r` is `&x`.
`int&&` binds **only** to rvalues (temporaries). Chapter 7: `std::move(x)` turns `x` into one.
`42` is a temporary, exactly what `int&&` accepts.

sections.title: Inside the function: what may the body do?
sections.rule: A parameter type is a **promise**. With `const T&` or `const T*` the body may only **read**. With `T* const` the local pointer can't be re-aimed (rarely useful). You can't **return** a non-const handle (`T&`, `T*`) to something you only received as const.
sections.prelude: struct Position { long qty; double price; };

cards.explanation: `p` is a read-only alias: you can't modify its members.
Reading through a `const&` is always fine. This is the right signature for a read-only function.
It compiles, but it modifies a **copy**: the caller's `Position` is unchanged. This was the bug in the const-correctness exercise's `scale`.
A non-const reference: the body modifies the caller's object. Use it when modifying is the function's job.
The `const` is left of `*`: the `Position` can't be modified through `p`.
The `Position` is protected, but the local pointer `p` (a copy of the caller's pointer) is not. Re-aiming it is allowed and has no effect on the caller.
`const` right of `*`: the pointer is fixed, but the pointee can be modified.
`p` is a const pointer, so it can't be re-aimed.
You can always make your **own** modifiable copy of something const.
A non-const alias of a const object would remove const.
Returning a non-const `Position&` would give the caller write access to something you only had read access to.
Const in, const out.
Same as in the exercise: a function given a `const Position*` can only hand back a `const Position*`.
Pointer arithmetic on a pointer to const gives another pointer to const.
As a parameter, `const Position ps[]` means **exactly** `const Position* ps` (array decay). The `[]` is only documentation.
It **compiles** (with a warning), but it returns a **dangling reference**: `local` dies when the function returns. Compiling is not the same as being correct.

sections.title: Function pointers and `std::function`
sections.rule: Start at the name and read outwards: `double (*f)(double)` reads "`f` is a pointer to a function taking a `double` and returning a `double`". The parentheses around `*f` are mandatory. A lambda **without captures** converts to a function pointer. `std::function` accepts anything that can be **called** with the right types.

cards.explanation: A function's name decays to a pointer to it, as an array's name does.
For functions the `&` is optional: `square` and `&square` both work.
Function pointer types must match **exactly**: `long(long)` is not `double(double)`.
Without the parentheses, this declares a **function** `f` returning `double*`, and a function can't be initialised.
Call through the pointer directly. `(*f)(3.0)` (the slides' spelling) means the same.

cards.code:
using Fn = double (*)(double);
Fn f = square;
cards.explanation: A type alias makes function pointer types readable. Recommended.
`std::function` can hold any callable with a compatible signature.

Surprise: `std::function` only needs the call to *work*. `double → long → double` conversions are implicit, so `twice` is accepted, with silent truncation! A raw function pointer refuses it (3rd card).
Here the call can't work: a `double` can't be passed as an `int*`, so `std::function` refuses it.
A lambda **with no captures** converts to a plain function pointer.

cards.code:
int k = 2;
double (*f)(double) = [k](double x) { return k * x; };
cards.explanation: A capturing lambda carries data (`k`), so it can't be a bare function pointer. Use `std::function` or `auto`.

cards.code:
int k = 2;
std::function<double(double)> f = [k](double x) { return k * x; };
cards.explanation: `std::function` can hold capturing lambdas: that's what it's for.
It compiles, but calling an **empty** `std::function` throws `std::bad_function_call` at run time.
